Tiger Gold Posts New Drill Results from the Ceibal Target
Tiger Gold reported new step-out drill results at its Colombia-based Ceibal target within its Quinchía gold project. 
Drilling at Ceibal showed a near continuous zone of gold mineralization from the surface all the way down to 707 meters, the bottom of the drill hole. The results included mineralization of:
23m @ 1.1 g/t Au
8m @ 1.0 g/t Au
2.2 g/t Au and 114 ppm molybdenum
10m @ 1.4 g/t Au
And these results are open at depth. 
Ceibal is shaping up to be a sizable deposit. So far, drilling has defined a strike length of at least 300 metres (still open in 3 directions) at a width of about 300 meters, and now open at depths below 700 meters. 
The Ceibal target is about 1 kilometer south of Tiger’s Miraflores deposit, and 1 kilometer southwest of its Tesorito deposit. 
Tiger currently has three drill rigs active across all three deposits, with assays pending from multiple targets. 
The company will continue to drill the rest of its initial 5,000 meter program at Ceibal with focus on more step out drilling and deeper holes. 
The goal is to publish a Mineral Resource Estimate once the initial drilling is completed.

text:
The general rule in microeconomics is that the optimum production rate is achieved when the marginal cost intersects the marginal revenue. The divergence to this rule has been dealt with in the last chapter, save to repeat that for a depleting resource with a defined life, the profit maximising moment for the Life of Mine is where costs are at a minimum. The optimal profit per annum is the point at which the marginal revenue and the marginal cost intersect. These two production moments provide tactical battery limits to adjust to factors such as price movements, grade variations or recovery issues, in the short run.
Bringing the two graphs together for comparative purposes is useful to demonstrate the optimal moments on the Total Cost Function for a firm and its unit cost derivative, i.e., the U-shaped cost curve. When individual cost curves are added to others within the industry, an aggregate industry cost curve results. Aggregate cost curves are used widely in the mining industry and are referred to as the industry cost curve. More attention will be paid to this in the next chapter, but highlighting the micro moments, apply equally on an industry scale, save for the absence of fixed costs seen in Figure 48.
- Points 1 and 2 in frame B are the breakeven levels of production. They correspond to the points in frame A, where the total revenue curve (TR) intersects the total cost curve (TC). Production above and below these points will result in economic losses and they are therefore the breakeven points.
- Point 3 is the minimum point on the ATC and is coincident with the MC bisecting it. This is the Life of Mine optimum level of production, described by Minnitt. It is also the point that describes the division between economies and diseconomies of scale. Beyond this point, the average unit costs of production begin to rise. This point corresponds to point 5 in frameA and a useful point of incidence when considering aggregate demand, the industry cost curve and price discovery.
- Point 4 is the intersection between the marginal cost (MC) and marginal revenue (MR) curves at which MC = MR. At this level of production, the slope of the total revenue curve (TR) is parallel to the total cost (TC) curve in frame A. This rate of production maximises net revenue (TR – TC) per year.

text:
“On cost side, unit cash costs are used rather than accounting costs that use depreciation and other non-cash cost items. Cash costs are the focus because the power of the cost curve focuses on the marginal producer, and when they receive enough marginal revenue to cover their out-of-pocket production costs or when they choose to exit, which is when the reverse is true. The relevant costs McKinsey & Company consider in their curve are: cash costs, transportation costs, working capital, and the cost of capital that is tied up in fixed and working capital, associated with the new capacity. If a producer is considering taking capacity off-line, closure cost is included. McKinsey states that the industry cost curve so formulated, is simply another representation of the classical microeconomic U-shaped cost, showing elasticity of demand. Once the costs have been arranged from lowest to highest, the next step is to identify the market demand level and place it on the curve, against the capacity that is available. The market demand line is represented as a vertical line, representing the market demand known at a point in time. The industry capacity to the left of the demand line is the most efficient capacity to meet the demand level, and the capacity to the right, represents the excess capacity or unneeded capacity to meet demand. The market price will be bracketed, in an equilibrium manner, between the supply unit where the demand line is going straight across, to the left, and the first unit of unneeded capacity in the market.”
McKinsey also suggests that the tool can be used in a predictive manner, but that caution must be taken when applied in a predictive way, to consider that uncertainty is introduced, leading to an uncertain range around price. The cost curve, from their perspective, is ideally suited for commodities, and fundamental in analysing the dynamics of pricing. By bringing greater microeconomic rigour to strategy formulation, mining companies can benefit from the insights relating to the market’s predicted price and profit sensitivities, notwithstanding their competitors’ actions. In principle, the industry cost curve allows companies to predict the impact of industry capacity, shifts in demand, and the influence that input costs have on market prices.
McKinsey’s cost curve has been widely adopted by the mining industry across a range of commodities, and the Holy Grail for miners is said to be a cost position within the first quartile of costs. Whilst these now standard curves are useful in measuring the relative competitive cost positions of miners, the construction of the S-shaped and U-shaped cost curves affords mining companies greater application and insights to optimise and maximise their extraction strategies and the core subject matter of this book.
A significant complexity is understanding that mining costs are largely driven by the quantities of ore mined and milled, rather than the metals produced. The significance of this is that in the world of mining, low-cost producers may report as relatively higher cost producers on the metal produced cost curve, if they do not benefit from either high-grade orebodies and/or non-high-grade by-product production. The industry cost curve widely used by investors and the industry largely disguises the costs of production, as higher-grade ore deposits or by- products minimise the cost of production. The risk is that management teams of well-endowed mineral deposits can operate less efficiently than their competitors, yet still maintain their competitive industry positioning. The application of microeconomic rigour is to cut through this noise and highlight an ore deposit’s inherent economic capacity and cost structure, based on the underlying cost drivers.
Nevertheless, however inefficient or efficient and/or well-endowed or poorly endowed an orebody being mined; the industry cost curve remains an important and useful market benchmark. For market analysts and investors, it provides relative market insight, into which mines and/or miners are most vulnerable, to price movement at varying price levels.
Fornero and Kircher (2018), succinctly defined the challenge: “The rise of the [copper] spot price in the mid-2000s, was not validated by higher forecasted prices on a medium to long-term horizon. Instead, it was considered as a transitory price increase, by the professional forecasters, who predicted that the spot price would return to values of around 100 cents. Due to the crisis (Global Financial Crisis), the price fell and almost reversed the rise from 2003 to 2007, reaching a minimum of approximately
140 cents (where the annual average understates somewhat the dynamic evolution of the spot price). That decline was relatively short-lived, and after the crisis, the copper price quickly recovered and exceeded its pre-crisis levels.
However, the higher post-crisis prices were also accompanied by higher forecasted prices, as part of a process of gradual forecast revisions, which had already started around 2007. In the following years, the forecasted prices reached values much closer to the effective spot price. Hence, the professional forecasters seem to have incorporated a more persistent price increase in their forecasts over time. More recently, as the commodity cycle has turned and prices have fallen, it has taken the forecasters again, several years, to adjust their expectations on future prices downwards.” In short, forecasters got it wrong and lagged the price trajectory.

The short version: the 8.6Moz is real, and the next catalyst (the maiden AurMac PEA, expected H2 2026) is fully funded. But there are many things the promotional layer glosses over. A few examples:
1. The "90%+ recovery" headline is the mill/CIL number. That points to a conventional mill build, plausibly C$1B-class capex, not the cheap heap-leach the ounce count might suggest. The story quietly shifts from "look how many ounces" to "who pays for the mill, and at what dilution."

And every new Yukon mine application now gets judged against the Eagle failure next door, a permitting and First Nation discount I'd argue is still underpriced here.
Asymmetry as priced (agent's speculation, not a filed number): roughly 1.5–2x up on a strong PEA versus 35–45% down on a weak one. Not the skew I want before economics exist.
The full report is once again bulky, but I suggest reading it all carefully. It works through the whole picture: the team's actual track record (named exits, not bios), deposit-by-deposit asset breakdown, the royalty stack, treasury and the share register (who really owns this and at what price), PEA scenario math instead of a single hopeful NPV, the post-Eagle permitting reality, catalysts, and a proper how-you-lose-money bear case.

Every figure is cited to the filing it came from. A few tastes of what's buried in there:

- Grade sequencing, not grade. Headline grade is 0.58–0.68 g/t, but there's a 2.45Moz indicated subset at ~1.00 g/t, and financeability hinges on whether the PEA schedules that material early enough to pay back a mill. No interview or promo deck gets into mine sequencing; here it's the whole ballgame.
- Who Alpayana actually is. The October 2025 raise wasn't generic paper: a Peruvian operating miner took the hard-dollar shares and back-ended the charity flow-through, and now sits at 8%. The same group just completed an all-cash takeover of Sierra Metals. Passive holder, development partner, or first bidder? The filings pose that question; no promo deck will.
- The endgame is a sale, and the report names the table. John Robins (Kaminak to Goldcorp, Great Bear to Kinross) added as strategic advisor, plus a VP Corp Dev hired from Probe Gold: a bench built to sell AurMac post-PEA, not self-build. The realistic buyer list writes itself from disclosed behavior: Kinross (~C$1.8B for Great Bear), Agnico (US$2.4B Hope Bay commitment), Fuerte (now owns Coffee down the road), Alpayana already on the register. But the report's punchline holds: a large resource plus a credible economic plan is acquirable. A large resource plus ugly capex is just a financing problem wearing a gold bull-market costume.

Triple Flag Acquires a $440 million Australian Stream

Triple Flag Precious Metals Corp announced a new gold stream acquisition on the Australia-based Ravenswood mine.

The structure of the stream:
5.50% of payable gold, stepping down to 3.75% after 194,200 oz delivered, then to 2.50% after 253,000 oz
Ongoing payment: 10% of spot gold price per ounce until 194,200 oz delivered, then 20% afterwards
First delivery: Q3 2026 — meaning this deal is immediately beneficial.

Triple Flag also holds a right of first offer on future Ravenswood streams/royalties — a foothold for follow-on deals

Ravenswood is a major gold asset, with 2.8 million ounces of proven and probable reserves, 3.6 million ounces of measured and indicated, and 1 million ounces of inferred resource.

The mine has produced gold for 150 years, with over 4 million ounces produced since 1868.

Montage improves gold resource estimates as it moves towards first production

Montage Gold Corp released an updated Mineral Resource Estimate on its Kone project - drastically increasing resource on the satellite gold deposits by over 1 million ounces.

The total Measured and Indicated resource now sits at over 6.29 million ounces - and the grade improved from 0.63 grams/tonne to 0.80 grams/tonne, which helps the overall economics of the project improve by 27% over the 2024 feasibility study’s estimates.

Mine construction remains on budget and ahead of schedule, and the company still projects the first gold production will occur late in 2026.

The company also projects that the type of mine being built for the main and satellite deposits is unprofitable below $2,500/ounce gold, which gives the company a huge margin of safety as gold still holds strong well over $4k/oz.
There is still exploration and drilling going on at some of the satellite deposits that could increase the M&I ounces and improve mine economics. The Petit Yao satellite, for instance, is just 7km from the main processing plant, and it currently has 319,000 ounces inferred at 1.28 grams/tonne. But the current Mineral Resource Estimate does not include all drilling and infill results on Petit Yao, as it’s still ongoing.

It’s an exciting time as Montage ramps up towards first production while it’s still expanding its gold resource estimates.

Montage expects more results this quarter and throughout the rest of the year from various satellite properties.

Verdict: WAIT. Not the orebody. Kamoa-Kakula is world-class. The catch is what actually reaches a shareholder:

- You don't own the copper. Ivanhoe's economic stake is just 39.6%, a minority slice of a stacked JV.
- Cash climbs through project debt, ~$1B of shareholder loans, and a gate releasing only 20% of profits.
- At ~$13.3B EV you're underwriting ~$5/lb+ long-term copper. That's a price bet, not a value entry.
The verdict is deliberately very skeptical (this is the right way to wire the AI agent imho; you don't want AI to be another stock pumper). But the report runs both sides in full. In a sustained high-copper world, the same sum-of-the-parts flips to a discount to NAV. I'm not here to call buy/sell. The goal is a complete intelligence slice on the stock, so you can reach your own answer.
I also tried to make the full report more readable, since it's very long (40+ pages), so I added a table of contents at the very beginning for easy navigation. There’s a narrative that the gold price and the USD index are inversely correlated, when the dollar rises, gold falls. I rarely see anyone who asserts this show any data to back it up.

This chart shows 25 years of history of the gold price with an overlay of the dollar index.

Clearly there are multi year periods where this is true, 2001-mid 2008 is one example. But from mid 2008-2011 the dollar was volatile and sideways but gold was up strongly.

From 2011-2016 the inverse correlation returned, dollar up, gold down.

From 2018-2025 the dollar and gold rose in tandem. A seven year period where the narrative failed.

Since Jan 2025, the correlation has returned.

There are periods of time where factors that favor the dollar are unfavorable to gold. And also many times when the dollar and gold follow the beat of different drummers.

text:
VIZSLA COPPER COMMENCES 2026 DRILL PROGRAM AT THE PALMER PROJECT
Vancouver, British Columbia, June 18, 2026 – Vizsla Copper Corp. (TSXV: VCU, OTCQB: VCUFF, FRANKFURT: 97E0) (“Vizsla Copper” or the “Company”) is pleased to report that diamond drilling has commenced at its Palmer VMS Project in Southeast Alaska.
The fully funded 2026 exploration program represents the first phase of a multi-year strategy designed to expand the Project's critical minerals resource base, evaluate new discovery opportunities, and advance the technical understanding of the broader Palmer district.
Two drill rigs are currently operating on site, with approximately 10,000 metres of drilling planned during the 2026 field season. Initial drilling is focused on the Palmer Deposit's South Wall Zone (see Figure 1), where previous drilling identified a high-grade copper-rich core within Zone 1, including some of the highest copper grades intersected on the property to date.
Craig Parry, Executive Chairman and CEO, commented:
"With drilling now underway, our team is focused on building upon the success of recent exploration at Palmer. The 2026 program is designed to expand high-grade mineralization at the South Wall Deposit while evaluating several priority targets across the district. As our geological understanding continues to improve, Palmer is increasingly demonstrating the scale, exploration upside, and critical minerals endowment that we believe distinguishes it as one of the premier exploration opportunities in Southeast Alaska."
 
Peter Mercer, Senior Vice President, Alaska, added:
" The 2026 program reflects a balanced approach between resource expansion and discovery while advancing the environmental and technical understanding of the Project. The drill rigs are currently focused on areas where previous drilling has returned some of the highest copper grades encountered on the property, while mountain crews prepare additional drill sites to evaluate the mineral potential between the Palmer and AG deposits. As the season progresses, our focus remains on safe operations, disciplined execution, and generating the technical information needed to better understand the full potential of the district."
2026 Program Now Underway 
The 2026 program combines resource growth, new discovery opportunities, and technical studies designed to further advance the Company's understanding of the Palmer district.  Diamond drilling will initially focus on the Palmer Deposit, where initial holes are testing high-priority targets within the South Wall system. This first phase of drilling is designed to further define and expand the high-grade copper-rich core identified within Zone 1 and improve confidence within existing mineralized Zones 2 and 3 through targeted infill drilling. 
Drilling later this season is planned at two priority exploration targets located between the existing deposits. The HG Prospect, located west of the Palmer Deposit, hosts significant copper-zinc-silver mineralization exposed over more than 600 metres of strike length and shares several geological characteristics with the South Wall mineralized system. 
The Waterfall Prospect, situated between the Palmer and AG deposits, represents an important target where geological, geochemical, and alteration characteristics suggest potential to add additional mineralization between the known deposits. 
Beyond these priority drill targets, the Company will continue evaluating several regional prospects across the broader Palmer district, including Mount Henry Clay, Christmas Creek, and other underexplored target areas. Follow-up field investigations will include geological and structural mapping, high-resolution photogrammetry, target refinement, and additional diamond drilling.
The exploration program is supported by an integrated technical initiative that includes advanced geological modelling, geophysical reinterpretation, critical minerals assessment, and continued environmental baseline studies. Together, these programs are intended to improve the Company's understanding of the Palmer district while supporting future technical, economic, and engineering studies.

text:
Some of us have argued in here about whether you can trust AI for real due diligence. One can argue AI can hallucinate, misrepresent, miss nuances, overstate.
Now I am going to make a comparison that may seem aggressive. But trust me, I have no intention to attack anyone or promote my work (the newsletter is free, I make nothing from it). I just want to share this observation for the sake of intellectual argument.
Here are two coverages of Banyan's June 17th drill results.

1. The first, produced by Jeff D (who I'm sure is an amazing writer and does great work). The article leads with a sensational headline and then does a fair job explaining the drill results. https://thegoldadvisor.com/the-gold-advisor/newsletters/banyan-gold-emperor-metals-video/

2. The second, produced by my custom AI workflow. The headline is less exciting. It agrees the hole is good, but it dives deep into the important nuances:

- Most of the grade in that headline interval is a single short 1.8 m sample. Strip it and the rest of the interval sits below the deposit's resource grade.
- The new high-grade is skarn-hosted, which is a metallurgy question, not a clean win, and it points toward a capital-intensive mill rather than a cheap heap leach.
- There is no recovery data in the release, so it does not actually touch the process-route and capex questions that feed the coming PEA and the NPV. https://assayer.substack.com/p/banyan-gold-bynv-drills-558-gt-at
Of course, I am not saying AI should replace the human analyst. I had to direct the agent and do the final human verification myself. And I believe the same tool in the hands of someone more technical and knowledgeable, like Jeff, would produce even more impressive results.

I just want to fight the superstition that AI must be shallow and unreliable. And as long as I see interest from you, I'll keep sharing my knowledge and work on mastering state-of-the-art AI tools.
Btw, just like Jeff, I am overweight Banyan and have no intention too sell either.

Theodoro Teixeira
Michael Gentile seems to agree with your tech market valuation.
Michaerl Gentile says ''…….This week I wanted to take you on a trip down memory lane...
I had a long conversation this week with my partner at Bastion Asset Management, Charles Haggar. He is the best investor I have ever met and he was incredibly frustrated by the lack of rationality in the market right now. As we flipped through chart after chart on his Bloomberg, I had such a strong sense of deja vu. It was like I had seen this movie before: the current mania around AI, Hyperscalers, Space X... it all reminds me so much of the 1997 to 2000 period during the dotcom bubble.
In the late 1990s, the Internet was going mainstream and was going to change the world. All investor attention moved to .com stocks as they were called back then. If you were not an internet stock, or had ties to the internet boom, you were considered "Old Economy" and largely of no interest to investors. Warren Buffet, the best investor of all time, was considered senile and past his prime because he refused to partake in the euphoria and buy these stocks.
Meanwhile, this emerging market country called China started to consume ever larger amounts of Oil, creating a massive demand tailwind for Oil in a period where Oil prices had been weak and depressed, and thus supply had shrunk. Despite the obvious signs of massive demand growing in the East for Oil, most investors were fast asleep, mesmerized by the internet bubble. Taxi drivers (now called Uber drivers) were trading internet stocks in their cars, and waitresses would tell customers what internet stocks they owned and how much money they had made that week on the market.
I will always remember in my last year of university (in 2000) right before the top, a deep value bottom up fundamental Portfolio Manager came to my class to make a presentation. He showed two very powerful slides: on one side was Nortel Networks, which at the time had the biggest market cap in Canada, and its single stock weight in the Index was 33% of the entire Toronto Stock Exchange; on the other side he had 20 of the largest and best known companies in the USA — Walmart, McDonalds, General Mills, Ford, etc. 
On the next slide he showed the revenues, profits, and free cash flow from the 20 largest American companies vs the lack of profits, free cash flow and much more modest revenues from Nortel. Then he said I will give you $300B dollars (back then $300B was a lot of money). You can either own this one stock or you can own 100% of all 20 of these businesses. Which do you want to buy??
Without the stock market screaming at us, without CNBC talking 24/7 about the internet and how it was going to change the world, the choice seemed clear as day. How could one company that was selling fibre optics (think the Nvidia of 1999) be worth more than 20 of the US's most profitable and largest companies? Why would I buy a business at 100 or more price to earnings when the best businesses in America at the time could be bought for 10X-14X earnings?
If you look at history you know how badly that movie ended. The Internet did change the world and was bigger than anyone ever dreamed at the time. BUT... Nortel went bankrupt and its partner in crime, Cisco Systems, went down 90% from the highs. Most of the Internet stocks that never made any money and traded on growth potential and end market opportunity went to zero.... 
Meanwhile, the Oil demand trade in China that nobody was paying attention to? Well, Oil went from $10 to $140 and Oil stocks were market-leading equities from 2002 to 2014.
What does this have to do with the mining business, you say? Well, today it is me that is the older, value-focused fund manager. And today I could make the very same slide that the fund manager presented to me over 25 years ago. On one side I could put companies like Nvidia ($5T market cap) and SpaceX ($3T market cap), and on the other side the entire mining industry, which is valued as of Q1 2026 at $2.5T.
So dear readers, I am giving you $2.5T today (it's your lucky day), and on one side you can buy 50% of Nvidia ($5T * 50%) or all of Space X ($2.5T) OR you can own every publicly traded mining company in the world! BHP, Newmont, Barrick, Rio Tinto, Glencore, Agnico, all the way down to Radisson and Capitan Silver. You can either own one half of a tech company or you can own the vast majority of all base metals and precious metals produced on an annual basis globally...
So, I could very much sympathize with my partner at Bastion Asset Management. When the market gets caught up in euphoria or a mania, like the .com boom, the nifty fifty in the 70s, or AI and Space X today, that sector often sucks up all the investor attention, all the market cap and liquidity in the market, leaving the profitable and essential business in the market, like metals and mining equities, deeply undervalued. 
When the AI / Space bubble bursts and the inevitable rotation out of AI stocks, Hyperscalers, and SpaceX happens, that money will look for a new home most likely in the most profitable and strongest positioned sectors (mining). The subsequent rotation into metals and mining could be very dramatic and powerful. So sell some Nvidia and SpaceX, grab some junior mining shares and some popcorn, and get ready for the sequel.

It should be a wild and fun ride. ''
-
Ed Yardini makes a good counter argument.
''The stock market bubble of the late 1990s was driven by fear of missing out (FOMO) on the tech-led bull market. As a result, the forward P/E of the S&P 500 rose to a record high of 25.0 in early 2000 as the forward P/E of the S&P 500 Information Technology sector soared to a record high of 55.0 (chart).
The current bull market has been increasingly driven by fabulous earnings momentum (FEMO). On Friday, the S&P 500 closed near its June 2 record high of 7609.78. Its forward P/E was 20.4, while the Information Technology sector's was just 23.0.
An earnings-led rally should be much more sustainable than a P/E-led one fueled by irrational exuberance. FEMO beats FOMO. The question that we are asked more often these days is whether the quality of earnings is eroding and fueling irrational exuberance in earnings expectations. Might circular financing be artificially boosting earnings among the AI-related companies? Might capital gains on their investments in one another be doing the same?………. ''

G2 Goldfields announced that its deal to merge G2 with G Mining Ventures was approved by the Ontario Superior Court. G2 Goldfields
The deal will now close in July 2026, and GUYGF shares will cease trading. For every delisted share of GUYGF, G2 share holders will receive 0.212 shares of G Mining, as well as 0.5 shares of a new spunoff company called G3 Goldfields. 
G2’s primary Guyana goldfields assets (the Oko properties),  will be owned by the newly merged G Mining company, while G2’s non-core assets will be held by G3. 
The merged company in G Mining has the potential to become a self-funded 700,000 oz/year operation, with most of the production coming out of the Oko properties.

Omai Gold Mines completed metallurgical testwork on its Wenot and Gilt deposits, confirming 93-95% recovery from standard CIL processing. 
It’s good news ahead of Omai’s upcoming Preliminary Economic Assessment, which is expected in the next 4-6 weeks. 
The high recovery rates from this testing also helped Omai revise its daily tonnage production upwards from 15,000-18,000 tonnes per day to 20,000-25,000 tonnes per day. 
That’s largely due to how cleanly and simply the CIL processing was able to extract gold. The specific qualities of the ore regardless of grade can sometimes decrease recovery rates and slow down the entire process. 
Higher ore throughput means more gold production with better economics. 
Omai continues to run a 50,000 meter drill program, focused on converting Wenot’s inferred resources to indicated resources (a higher level of certainty). 
The company also plans on completing a Feasibility Study in 2027, based largely on the results of its PEA, coming late July/early August.
